<reason>Elite, genuinely contested debate. B built the cleaner intuitive frame (write rules vs. contest their application; "who holds the wrench") and answered the unit fork reasonably. But B staked the round on durability via the labor exemption (B1.5, "the point that should decide the round"), and A severed that link: B's decisive feasibility mechanism turned out to be voluntary conference recognition — which A showed is (a) management's permission, cutting against B's anti-unilateralism core, and (b) incapable of earning the labor exemption absent employee status, a hit B never answered in any later speech. A also directly answered both pressure questions with proper A1/A2 labels, while B's Rebuttal 2 claimed "silence" on questions whose designated answer slot (Turn 8) had not yet occurred in the actual chronology — a misdescription falsified by A's very next speech. A's closing then turned B's own "setting terms" test against B (permission-gated table, immunized cap). Both sides were well-grounded with no fake precision; symmetric minor clipping. A converted more pressure into concessions and left fewer live attacks unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8): after cleanly answering Q1/Q2, it converted B's own answers into concessions — the "unit follows the money" shrinks the motion to two men's teams (plus an unanswered Title IX problem), and "voluntary recognition" means the table exists by the school's consent and, without employee status, delivers no labor exemption, collapsing the durability rationale B called decisive.</best_rebuttal>
